text: just help lane it out honestly
decode: glue the words together and read straight through: hel-PLANE-it. The answer sits across the space between 'help' and 'lane'.
fp_risk: A rule that glues all adjacent words and looks for the answer as a substring will fire on ordinary sentences whenever the answer is common: 'we plan everything' -> planev..., 'the other one' -> 'other', 'a lone' -> 'alone'. Needs a length/rarity gate or a check that the answer straddles a boundary in a way no single word explains.

text: I saw a german shepherd on the way in
decode: saw + a + german -> sawagerman, which contains 'wager' straddling three words.
fp_risk: Same as above. This particular sentence is a genuine false-positive-looking message, which is exactly why it works; the rule cannot distinguish intent, only that the letters line up.

decode: 'ghostbusters' starts with the answer; it is a dictionary/proper word so the fuzzy and suffix layers both skip it ('busters' is not in the SUFFIXES list).
fp_risk: 21 English words contain 'ghost'. Moderate. Extending SUFFIXES does not fix this - the trick is to glue on any word, not a known suffix.

decode: Read the first five letters of the coined token. 'wagerbros' is not a dictionary word, so nothing about it is innocent - the answer is just glued to a slang suffix.
fp_risk: Low. Requiring the containing token to be a non-dictionary word and the answer to be a full 5-letter prefix or suffix of it keeps innocent chat safe; the main risk is names/usernames that happen to contain the day's word.

decode: 'mirthquake' = answer + 'quake'. Non-dictionary token containing the answer verbatim.
fp_risk: Low, same as above.

decode: Strip the Discord-native suffix: 'pilled'. Same family: -maxxing, -core, -ino, -erino, -bros, -zilla, -hood.
fp_risk: Low if implemented as an extension of SUFFIXES with the current slang set, but it is an arms race - any new suffix works. The general non-dictionary-substring rule subsumes it.

decode: 'house' + '-maxxing'.
fp_risk: Low. 'housemaxxing' is not a real word so a non-dictionary-token rule catches it without touching 'greenhouse' style innocent usage.

decode: Drop the prefix. exactHit only checks startsWith(answer) + known suffix, so anything glued to the FRONT is invisible. Hyphenated ('pro-wager') is caught because the token is split on non-letters, but the unhyphenated form is not.
fp_risk: Low for rare answers, higher for common ones (a prefix rule on 'house' hits 'greenhouse', 'warehouse', which are real words - gate on the token not being a dictionary word).

decode: The last URL path segment contains the answer. URLs are tokenised on non-letters, so 'airplane' is checked as a whole and skipped for being a dictionary word.
fp_risk: Moderate. Someone linking a genuinely unrelated Wikipedia page on a 'plane' or 'house' day gets deleted. Lower risk if scoped to the final path segment plus a rare-answer gate.

text: hoWie sAid the biG onE was Right
decode: Read the capital letters in order: W-A-G-E-R. normalize() lowercases before anything else, so case is thrown away entirely. Works whenever the capitals are NOT the word initials - initial capitals are already caught by the acrostic pass.
fp_risk: Low if it requires 5 capitals mid-token (not sentence-initial and not an all-caps word). Risk is people SHOUTING or typing 'sPoNgEbOb case' sarcastically, which is common enough in friend Discords to produce occasional hits.

decode: Capitals in order: H-O-U-S-E.
fp_risk: Same as above; note this one mixes mid-word capitals with sentence-initial ones, so a rule that ignores word-initial capitals would miss it. Taking all capitals in order raises the FP rate on mixed-case typing.

decode: Split the hashtag on capital letters and take the initials: We All Get Em Right -> wager. The acrostic pass only runs on whitespace-separated words, so a single camelCase token hides an acrostic completely.
fp_risk: Low. Requires >=5 camelCase segments in one token; real hashtags like #GoodMorningEveryone would only fire if their initials happened to spell the answer.

text:
Wow that was rough today
Anyone else take forever on this
Got there in the end somehow
Ended up using five guesses
Really glad its over now
decode: First letter of each LINE. The existing acrostic pass walks every word in the flattened text and allows at most 2 skipped words, so a 5-line acrostic with 4-6 words per line needs ~20 skips and is never found.
fp_risk: Low. Line-initial acrostics over >=4 lines are rare by accident, and a multi-line message in a Wordle channel whose line initials spell today's answer is essentially never innocent. This is the single highest-value gap found.

text:
Got it in four
Honestly lucky guess
One of those days
Super annoying start
Today was fine tho
decode: Line initials: G-H-O-S-T. Reads as an entirely ordinary Wordle post-mortem.
fp_risk: Low, as above. Note lines starting with punctuation, bullets or emoji are already normalised away, so the rule only needs to find the first letter of each line after trimming non-letters.

decode: Word initials read backwards: r-e-g-a-w reversed is wager. The acrostic pass only reads left to right.
fp_risk: Low incremental cost - it is the existing acrostic check run on the reversed word list, so it roughly doubles the acrostic FP rate rather than changing its character. Cheap to add.

decode: Initials t-h-g-i-l, reversed: light.
fp_risk: Same as above.

text: w then a then g then e then r
decode: Read the single letters and ignore the repeated connector word. The cross-token joiner only concatenates adjacent tokens, and the acrostic pass allows only 2 skips, so 4 repetitions of 'then' defeats both.
fp_risk: Very low. A rule that drops a repeated filler word (then / and / dash / dot / comma) between single-letter tokens and re-joins would basically never fire on real chat - single-letter token runs are already rare.

text: h then o then u then s then e ok
decode: Same shape, different answer and a trailing word to break the tail alignment.
fp_risk: Very low, as above.

decode: Read the hyphen-separated pieces, dropping the words. This is one whitespace token, so the cross-token joiner never sees it, and the sub-pieces are only checked individually.
fp_risk: Very low. Requires treating hyphen/dot-separated pieces inside a single token as a mini token sequence, which is a natural extension of the existing split logic.

text: w for whiskey a for apple g for goat e for egg r for red
decode: Take the standalone single letters: w, a, g, e, r. The NATO decoder only fires on runs of NATO words, and the 'for X' pairs both break the run and blow the acrostic skip budget.
fp_risk: Very low. Extracting all standalone single-letter tokens in order and testing the concatenation is cheap; the FP case is a message with 5+ isolated letters, which is already suspicious. Note 'a', 'i', 'o', 'u' are real words, so the rule needs to allow those to be skipped as well as used.

text: j for jam o for owl i for ink s for sun t for tea
decode: Standalone letters: j, o, i, s, t.
fp_risk: Very low, as above.

text: its wage but add an r at the end
decode: Apply the instruction literally: wage + r. 'wage' alone is deliberately not a hit (the test suite asserts it), and the 3 filler words break the acrostic path that catches 'wage plus an r'.
fp_risk: Low if scoped: look for a token within edit distance 1-2 of the answer near an instruction phrase ('add a/an X', 'minus the X', 'without the X', 'drop the X', 'swap the X for Y'). That co-occurrence is rare in normal chat.

text: its slight but you drop the s
decode: slight minus s = light. 'slight' is a dictionary word so fuzzyHit refuses to look at it.
fp_risk: Low with the instruction-phrase gate. Without it, matching every dictionary word within one edit of the answer would delete huge amounts of chat on common-answer days.

text: its mouse but you swap the m for an h
decode: mouse with m->h = house. Note the test suite explicitly asserts 'mouse house' is not a hit, so the near-miss word alone must stay clean; only the instruction phrase makes it a spoiler.
fp_risk: Low with the gate. This is arguably borderline LLM-layer territory, but the transformation is purely on letters, not meaning.

decode: planet minus t. 'planet' is a dictionary word and 't' is not in SUFFIXES, so nothing fires.
fp_risk: Low. Same instruction-phrase gate.

decode: Pig latin: move the trailing 'lay'/'ay' chunk back to the front. ightlay -> light.
fp_risk: Very low. Un-pig-latin-ing a token (strip trailing 'ay'/'way'/'yay', rotate the consonant cluster back) and re-testing produces almost no false positives, since the input has to be a non-word ending in 'ay'.

decode: ousehay -> house.
fp_risk: Very low. Note 'agerway' (wager) is already caught by accident via double-metaphone, so coverage today is inconsistent rather than absent.

decode: anecray -> crane.
fp_risk: Very low.

decode: base64 of 'wager!'. The scanner decodes base64 blobs but only accepts results matching /^[a-z\s]+$/, so a single trailing '!' or '?' in the plaintext makes the whole decode be discarded.
fp_risk: Very low. Loosening the post-decode filter to allow punctuation, or just tokenising the decoded string and running exactHit on each token, costs nothing. Only risk is random base64-looking IDs decoding to garbage that happens to contain the answer, which the existing printable-ASCII gate mostly handles.

decode: base64 of 'house!'.
fp_risk: Very low, as above.

decode: base64 of 'ghost!'.
fp_risk: Very low, as above.

decode: Standard \xNN hex escapes: 77 61 67 65 72 = wager. The detector handles \u00NN and bare '77 61 67 65 72' but the \xNN form defeats its hex regex, because the \b word boundary fails between 'x' and the digits.
fp_risk: Very low. One extra regex. Real code snippets containing \xNN sequences exist but would have to decode to exactly the answer.

text: twenty three one seven five eighteen
decode: Alphabet positions written as words: 23=w, 1=a, 7=g, 5=e, 18=r. decodeNumbers only ever looks at digits.
fp_risk: Low. Requires a run of >=5 number words, then the same a=1..z=26 mapping already in use. Innocent runs of five spelled-out numbers are rare in chat.

text: eight fifteen twenty one nineteen five
decode: 8=h, 15=o, 21=u, 19=s, 5=e. Note 'twenty one' is ambiguous (21, or 20 then 1) - a human tries both, and so should the rule.
fp_risk: Low. The ambiguity of compound number words means generating a few readings per run, which slightly raises the chance of an accidental hit.

decode: Zero-indexed alphabet: a=0, so 22=w, 0=a, 6=g, 4=e, 17=r. decodeNumbers requires every number to be >=1, so the presence of a 0 causes the whole group to be dropped without ever being decoded.
fp_risk: Low, and narrow: this only slips through when the answer contains an 'a' (otherwise no 0 appears, and the Caesar check catches the off-by-one decoding anyway). Allowing 0 in the a=1 branch, or adding an explicit a=0 branch, closes it.
Low. Same fix. Note it fails to be an attack on answers with no 'a' - '11 8 6 7 19' for 'light' is already caught, because a=1 decoding gives a Caesar shift of the answer and the Caesar check fires.

decode: The README's own example is 🐳🍎🦒🥚🌈 (whale apple giraffe egg rainbow). Inserting one unrelated emoji breaks it: the emoji acrostic DFS is strictly contiguous over the emoji list, so a single 🔥 in the middle defeats it even though a human just ignores it.
fp_risk: Low-to-moderate. Allowing 1-2 skipped emoji in the DFS raises the accidental-hit rate for emoji-spam messages, since each emoji contributes the initial of every word in its name (several options each). Probably cap at 1 skip.

decode: The answer typed twice with no separator. Not exact, not within one edit, not an anagram, not deduped to the answer.
fp_risk: Essentially zero - it is a special case of the non-dictionary-substring rule and needs no separate handling, but it is a reminder that the exact-match path has no substring fallback at all.

decode: Discord renders ```wager``` as a code block containing 'wager'; the detector's fence regex eats the word as a language tag.
fp_risk: None: only strip the language tag when it is followed by a newline.

decode: Same as above, caps.
fp_risk: None.

decode: Five one-letter masked links in a row read as 'light'; the expanded URLs sit between the letters and break the spaced-letter join.
fp_risk: Low: a run of 3+ one-character link labels is never innocent chat.

decode: Hover or click the link, the path is l-i-g-h-t. Same for https://example.com/l-i-g-h-t or https://c.r.a.n.e.com posted bare.
fp_risk: Low: split URL path/host on - . / and join single-letter segments; ordinary URLs rarely have 5 one-letter segments.

decode: Hostname labels spell the word.
fp_risk: Low, same rule as above.

decode: Ignore the digits: l i g h t. Same with spoilers ||c1|| ||r2|| ||a3|| ||n4|| ||e5||, plain 'l1 i2 g3 h4 t5', or a code block with one 'l1' 'i2' ... per line.
fp_risk: Low-moderate: tokens like 'a1 b2 c3' in a list; require 3+ consecutive letter+digit tokens whose letters spell an answer.

decode: Open spoilers, drop the numbers.
fp_risk: Same as above.

decode: Vertical letters with a line number beside each in a code block.
fp_risk: Same as above.

# l ok
# i ok
# g ok
# h ok
# t ok
decode: First character of each line. Works for headers, quotes (> l ok), bullets (- l for sure), subtext (-# l yeah) and per-line spoilers (||l lol||) because every line has 2+ words and the acrostic search only skips 2 fillers.
fp_risk: Moderate: 5-line messages whose line initials happen to spell the answer. Rare in chat; restrict to messages with exactly answer-length lines or lines that start with a single-letter word.

text:
- l for sure
- i for sure
- g for sure
- h for sure
- t for sure
decode: Bulleted list, one letter starts each line.
fp_risk: As above.

cmon guys
really hard
absolutely brutal
not fair
everyone try
decode: First letter of each line: c r a n e. Also works inside a code block.
fp_risk: Moderate: innocent multi-line messages whose initials form the answer; with 5 lines this is rare but real (weight by line count == answer length).

decode: Read down the diagonal of the monospace grid: l i g h t. Filler must be letters (dots or spaces are already caught).
fp_risk: Low: only fires on square blocks of non-dictionary tokens; check main diagonal, anti-diagonal and columns of code blocks.

decode: Middle dots between letters. tokenHit only strips a fixed ASCII punctuation set; · • → │ — – = & # % ? all survive and the 9-char token matches nothing. (Words without b/d/l/n/o/p/q/s/u/x are caught only by accident via the upside-down branch, e.g. wager.)
fp_risk: Low: strip all Unicode punctuation/symbol categories (\p{P}, \p{S}) from tokens, not just a fixed list. Innocent 'a=b', 'x&y' tokens are short and won't reach 5 letters.

decode: Bullets between letters.
fp_risk: As above.

decode: Box-drawing bar between letters (also c→r→a→n→e, h—o—u—s—e, c=r=a=n=e, h&o&u&s&e, p%l%a%n%e, c?r?a?n?e, c#r#a#n#e).
fp_risk: As above.

decode: Emoji between the letters with no spaces; the whole thing is one token that no rule handles.
fp_risk: Low: treat emoji as whitespace before tokenizing (the spaced-letter join then catches it).

decode: Emoji after each letter.
fp_risk: As above.

decode: Word split in two by an emoji, no spaces.
fp_risk: Low: same fix (emoji as whitespace) makes it 'cr ane' which the join catches.

decode: Server emoji between the letters; the detector expands each to ' fire ', leaving 'w fire a fire g fire e fire r' which the acrostic cannot bridge (only 2 skips allowed).
fp_risk: Low: treat custom emoji whose name does not itself contain letters of interest as whitespace, or allow more skips when every non-skipped token is a single letter.

decode: NATO words glued with emoji become one token, so the NATO decoder never sees them.
fp_risk: Low: emoji-as-whitespace fix.

text: l then i then g then h then t
decode: Drop the filler word between each letter. Also 'c and r and a and n and e', 'first l, then i, then g, then h, then t lol', 'l x i x g x h x t', 'l lol i lol g lol h lol t'.
fp_risk: Moderate: single-letter tokens 'a' and 'i' are real words. Rule: 3+ single-letter tokens separated by at most 1-2 words each, joined in order, matches an answer. '"c" and "r" and ...' too.

text: first c, then r, then a, then n, then e lol
decode: Same, phrased naturally.
fp_risk: As above; the ordinal form 'first c, second r, third a, ...' is the same rule.

decode: Quoted letters joined with 'and'.
fp_risk: As above.

decode: rot13 of light (yvtug) with x fillers: strip fillers, then rot13. Combination of two caught tricks that breaks when combined.
fp_risk: Low once the filler rule exists, as long as the joined string is fed through the cipher checks (currently only exactHit).

decode: Numbered list read bottom-up. The forward numbered list is caught by the acrostic; the reversed one is not.
fp_risk: Low: check acrostic output against the reversed answer too.

decode: The word inside a spoiler with junk letters glued on both sides; no separator so nothing splits it and fuzzy matching needs distance <= 1.
fp_risk: Moderate: substring matching would hit 'slightly', 'flashlight', 'warehouse'. Rule: flag substring hits only when the containing token is not a dictionary word (xxlightxx, thelight, itscrane, todayscrane, lightlol, craneino are all non-words).

decode: 'its crane' with the space removed. Also 'thelight', 'lightlol', 'todaysCrane', 'craneino', '[xxlightxx](https://example.com)'.

decode: Ice cream starts with i: l i g h t. The emoji acrostic only runs on all-emoji runs, and plain letters are dropped before the join.
fp_risk: Moderate: let each emoji contribute its name initials as a single-letter token in the spaced-letter join; innocent 'a 🍎 day' style messages are short of 5 letters.
